s: Today's theme is emotions and character.
We have ten advanced words for describing how people feel and how they behave.
These are exactly the words that separate an intermediate speaker from an advanced one.
When you can describe a personality precisely, people listen differently.
It is an adjective for someone who changes suddenly and unpredictably, especially in mood or plans.
My old boss was capricious with deadlines.
On Monday the report was due Friday, and by Wednesday morning it was due that afternoon.
That kind of capricious management destroys trust.
People stop planning because the plan never survives the week.
Capricious weather does the same thing to picnics.
I have cancelled three this year alone because the forecast changed overnight.
Her capricious moods were famous in the office.
Nobody knew which version of her would walk through the door.
The advanced move is using capricious for markets, weather, and people alike.
Anything that refuses to stay predictable earns this word.
A stoic person endures pain or hardship calmly, without complaining and without showing much emotion.
My grandfather was stoic about his illness.
He never once complained, even on the hardest days.
There is real dignity in a stoic reaction, but it can also worry the people around you.
They wonder what you are hiding.
He stayed stoic through the layoffs and spent his last weeks helping younger colleagues rewrite their resumes.
Being stoic is not the same as being cold.
It is choosing to carry your feelings quietly instead of handing them to everyone.
You can also be too stoic.
If you never show pain, people stop asking how you are.
As a noun, it means a deep, thoughtful sadness, often without any clear cause.
Autumn always brings a quiet melancholy for me.
The short days, the falling leaves, it all feels beautifully sad.
There is a sweet side to melancholy.
It slows you down and makes you notice things you would otherwise rush past.
After the concert ended, a wave of melancholy hit him.
He sat in his car for twenty minutes, not wanting the night to end.
Her melancholy lifted the moment her sister arrived.
Sometimes sadness just needs company, not solutions.
It is softer, more reflective, and honestly a little poetic.
It means childishly bad-tempered or sulky, especially over small things.
His petulant tone made the whole dinner awkward.
He was upset because his football team had lost a match.
A petulant outburst in a meeting can undo years of a good reputation.
People remember the tantrum long after they forget the apology.
She sounded petulant when the restaurant ran out of her favorite dessert.
It was honestly funny, and also a little embarrassing for everyone.
Do not be petulant about the performance review.
The feedback was fair, even if it stung at the time.
Petulant behavior is usually a sign of tiredness.
That rule has saved me many times.
It describes someone who enjoys the company of others, someone sociable and outgoing.
Her gregarious personality lights up every party.
Strangers become friends within minutes around her.
Gregarious people make the best hosts.
They introduce guests to each other and keep the conversation moving all evening.
My most gregarious colleague knows everyone's coffee order.
It sounds small, but it makes the whole team feel like family.
Even gregarious people need quiet time.
Being social takes energy, even when you genuinely love it.
A gregarious nature is a real gift in a new city, where you arrive knowing no one and have to build a life from zero.
It means quiet and unwilling to talk much about your feelings or opinions.
He was reticent about the real reasons he left the company.
We only learned the full story a year later.
My reticent neighbor rarely speaks, but when she does speak, every single word counts.
Being reticent is not the same as being rude.
Some people simply process everything internally before they share it.
Her reticent smile told us she knew more than she was saying, but she was not going to say it.
A reticent style can be surprisingly powerful in negotiations.
Silence makes the other side nervous and generous.
It means cheerfully optimistic about the future, even when the present looks difficult.
Despite the setbacks, she stayed sanguine about the launch.
Her confidence calmed the entire team.
A sanguine outlook is a leadership superpower.
People naturally follow optimism and run from despair.
His sanguine forecast for the economy sounded almost naive at first, but three of his four predictions actually came true.
I try to stay sanguine before exams.
Panic has never once improved my score, so optimism is the better strategy.
It is hard to stay sanguine after a rejection letter, but the people who manage it are usually the ones who eventually succeed.
As a noun, it means a strong feeling of contempt, a real lack of respect for someone or something.
He looked at the cheap imitation with open disdain and walked straight past it without slowing down.
Her disdain for small talk is legendary.
She would rather discuss one big idea than ten updates about the weather.
The review was dripping with disdain.
The critic clearly felt the movie was beneath serious discussion.
Masking disdain is an important social skill, especially when you are dealing with difficult clients.
Disdain always leaks out eventually, usually in your tone of voice.
It means feeling angry and bitter because you believe you have been treated unfairly.
She grew resentful after years of being passed over for promotion, and honestly, who could blame her.
Resentful employees do not complain loudly.
They go quiet, and that quiet is always the warning sign.
He felt resentful when his idea was presented as someone else's work.
That kind of theft stings for years.
A resentful tone crept into her voice every single time the new policy came up in conversation.
The only cure for feeling resentful is saying what you need before the bitterness has time to set in.
Our tenth and final word is nonchalant.
It means calm and relaxed in a way that can seem careless or unconcerned.
He gave a nonchalant shrug when they announced the delay, as if two extra hours meant absolutely nothing to him.
Her nonchalant attitude toward the deadline worried me at first, but she delivered the project a full day early.
He tried to look nonchalant before the interview, but his tapping foot completely gave him away.
A nonchalant entrance can be genuinely powerful.
Walking in calmly tells the room that you belong there.
Do not mistake her nonchalant style for laziness.
She simply refuses to perform stress for an audience.
Before we recap, let us play with pairs, because these words get sharper in contrast.
A stoic person is calm because they are strong.
A nonchalant person is calm because they are simply not bothered.
Your friend who forgot your birthday can afford to be nonchalant, but you will not love it.
Petulant is loud and short-lived, like a spark.
Resentful is quiet and long-lived, like rust.
A petulant colleague slams a door today and apologizes tomorrow.
A resentful colleague says nothing for a year and then quits without warning.
Both damage teams, but resentment is the one managers should fear.
You cannot fix a feeling that nobody will name.
Melancholy looks backward with tender sadness.
Sanguine looks forward with bright confidence.
The same rainy Sunday can produce melancholy in one person and a sanguine plan for the week in another.
And capricious deserves a partner too.
A gregarious friend makes ten new plans to replace the one you lost.
That is the beauty of a gregarious circle.
It absorbs the damage of capricious behavior, because there is always another dinner, another invitation, another evening.
Disdain is loud inside and leaks outside.
A reticent person holds everything inside, including admiration.
So a reticent colleague might respect you deeply and never show it, while a colleague full of disdain might smile politely and still leak contempt.
Which is why we read tone, not just words.
Ten words, five pairs, and every pair tells a small story about human nature.
Here is a challenge for our listeners.
Pick three of today's words and describe someone you know.
My uncle is gregarious at every wedding, completely stoic at every funeral, and quietly sanguine about everything in between.
Capricious with repairs, petulant about rent paid one day late, and full of disdain for anyone who questioned him.
That is a perfect character sketch in three words.
That is exactly what this vocabulary is for.
Not showing off, just seeing people clearly.
When you can name melancholy instead of just feeling blue, or spot resentful silence instead of just sensing tension, you understand the room faster.
And understanding the room is half of every negotiation, interview, and relationship.
Let us do a quick recap so these words stick.
Stoic means calm and uncomplaining under pressure.
Melancholy is a deep, thoughtful sadness.
Petulant means childishly sulky over small things.
Resentful means bitter about unfair treatment.
And nonchalant means calmly, almost carelessly, unconcerned.
Use all ten this week in real conversation and they will stay with you forever.
That is it for today's Word Kitchen.
We will see you next time.
